title: Learning Process Rewards via Visitation Matching for Efficient RL
claim: Turn sparse outcome labels into a dense learned process reward, then use it to finetune policies quickly, including in the real world.
layout: 4 panels, left-to-right, stage labels on top, real-world photo at right
description: A rounded gray box holds three cartoon panels, with a separate fourth panel at the right. Above the gray box, two pill-shaped labels, 'Discriminator Training' and 'RL Finetuning', are linked by bent arrows to show the order of the stages. Panel (a) shows a robot arm with dotted trajectories to a tomato, corn and pepper. The tomato and corn have red X marks and the pepper has a green check, labeled r^out. Panel (b) shows the same arm with a red blurred gradient toward the failed objects and a green gradient toward the pepper, labeled r^svm. Panel (c) shows the arm following a single dotted path along a green glow to the pepper. A large arrow leads to panel (d), a real photo of a robot gripper moving corn to a pot, with a dashed green path and the goal text above it.
caption: (a) Given trajectories labeled with sparse outcome reward rout, we train a discriminator to distinguish between state-actions in successful vs. unsuccessful trajectories. (b) This yields a dense process reward—the success visitation matching reward rsvm—that rewards visiting state-actions likely to be in successful trajectories. (c) Finetuning a policy with RL on a combination of the process reward and outcome reward enables fast RL improvement. (d) Our approach scales to real-world robotic control settings, enabling fast real-world RL.
abstract: In many modern applications of reinforcement learning (RL), the natural reward for a task of interest is inherently sparse: a reward of 0 is given everywhere except when the task is completed, when a reward of +1 is given. Training a policy to maximize such a sparse reward requires solving a challenging credit assignment problem, leading to slow or ineffective RL improvement. We propose a simple approach to transform a sparse outcome reward into a dense process reward. Our approach relies on training a discriminator to distinguish between previous successful and unsuccessful episodes, and using this discriminator to incentivize the RL-learned policy to match the state-action visitations of successful episodes, while avoiding those of unsuccessful episodes. By incentivizing the policy to match the visitations over all states, not just those that correspond to task success, this reward provides dense feedback on whether progress is being made towards task completion, and, we show, provably achieves this without changing the optimal policy. Focusing on finetuning of robotic control policies, we demonstrate that our approach leads to significantly faster RL finetuning performance on both simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, as compared to simply maximizing the sparse outcome reward.
